disease-biology|rabbit.summary: Tarandovskiy et al. 2020: Rabbit thrombin and plasmin generation were substantially lower than humans — thrombin peak 71.6 nM (15% of human 484.3), thrombin production 14.93 nM/min (13% of human 111.5); plasmin peak 197.7 nM (43% of human 457.2), plasmin production 17.63 nM/min (51% of human 34.8). Authors note high variability in rabbit plasmin-generation (PG) curves.

disease-biology|pig.summary: Mixed evidence: Tarandovskiy et al. 2020 found swine thrombin peak 242.35 nM (≈50% of human 484.25; n=20) and thrombin production rate 93.6 nM/min (≈84% of human 111.51), but plasmin was not detected in swine while human plasmin peak is 457.2 nM. Ranjan et al. 2025 cautions animal models vary in recapitulating human disease and highlights primates as more translatable, limiting pig applicability for human neurodevelopmental disease.

disease-biology|horse.summary: Oreff et al. 2021: horse tenocytes match human gene-expression under transient inflammation (Mahalanobis 9.59) and approximate human wound-closure kinetics (migration slope diff 0.0133 vs human, healthy). However they diverge in proliferation under healthy conditions (slope diff 0.3000, p<2e-16).

disease-biology|c. elegans.summary: Zong et al. 2023: C. elegans shows modest transcriptomic resemblance to human inflammatory disease—most within-stage cross‑species genome‑wide c-scores >0.1, though some pairs were lower (ce.lar–dm.lar c=0.087). Human–human c-scores reached up to 0.52 and some human pairs were ≈0, so similarity varies by comparison.

disease-biology|d. melanogaster.summary: Evidence shows D. melanogaster has low cross-species transcriptome resemblance in disease-related comparisons (Zong et al. 2023): most within-stage Drosophila–C. elegans genome-wide c-scores were >0.1, but one ce.lar–dm.lar pairing was 0.087. The study reports mainly invertebrate cross-species comparisons, not direct Drosophila–human matches.

disease-biology|mouse.summary: Evidence is mixed: Seok et al. 2013 found very low whole‑transcriptome concordance (R^2 ≤0.09, mouse vs human), whereas Takao et al. 2015 reported moderate–strong similarity (Spearman 0.43–0.68; 77–93% genes same direction). Disease‑ and method‑specific studies (Asgharpour et al. 2016 FDR 0.02; Holland et al. 2022 recall 0.40) show better but variable alignment.

disease-biology|mouse.why_range_is_wide: Ranges reflect different diseases, analysis choices and thresholds (whole‑transcriptome vs top/filtered genes), and model conditions/duration.

disease-biology|non-human primate.summary: Evidence is mixed: NHPs mirror some human physiology (baboon thrombin peak 434 nM vs human 484 nM; plasmin peak 546–566 nM vs human 457 nM). However, across disease studies animals overpredicted benefit (67–80% NHP trials improved vs 32% human) and animal PD models found 10% vs 36% human PD genes.

disease-biology|non-human primate.why_range_is_wide: Ranges reflect different NHP species, assays and trial subsets (e.g., 67–80% across NHP trial subsets; 546–566 nM plasmin across baboon vs rhesus).

disease-biology|rat.summary: Evidence is mixed: rats recapitulate many systemic and behavioral disease features — e.g., 26/30 blood biochemistry changes post‑exercise matched humans (magnitude 7.9% vs 7.3%; Goutianos et al. 2015) and cognitive/EEG markers paralleled human patterns (Der‑Avakian et al. 2025). However, transcriptomic concordance in Parkinson's models was negative (average concordance −0.04) and animal meta‑analysis recovered 10% vs 36% PD‑associated genes in humans (Oerton et al. 2017).

disease-biology|rat.why_range_is_wide: Alignment varies strongly by domain (transcriptomics vs systemic biochemistry vs behavior vs coagulation), model type and measured endpoints.

disease-biology|sheep.summary: Oreff et al. 2021: Sheep tenocyte gene-expression and proliferation match human responses mainly under constant inflammation (Mahalanobis 8.94; proliferation slope diff -0.0878, p=0.009) but are less similar when healthy (Mahalanobis 24.78) and only borderline under transient inflammation. Data are from three biological replicates per species.

efficacy|dog.summary: Martić-Kehl et al. 2012 found animal efficacy often did not predict human outcomes: fewer than 50% of animal studies predicted human results and only 3 of 494 animal-positive acute ischemic stroke interventions showed convincing patient benefit. Findings aggregate multiple species and indications, not dogs alone.
efficacy|dog.direction: evidence does not favour the model

efficacy|cattle.summary: Pound et al. 2018: animal–human concordance in cattle was mixed — 2 interventions (bisphosphonates, thrombolytics) concordant, 3 (corticosteroids, Tirilazad, antifibrinolytics) discordant and 1 partially concordant (antenatal corticosteroids). Under Bateson's Cube <7% of studies were permissible and some concordant results involved high animal suffering.

disease-biology|rodent.summary: Evidence shows rodent disease models often report preclinical benefit that does not mirror human outcomes: 90% of mouse and 95% of rat preclinical trials reported apparent improvement versus 32% of human trials (Marshall et al. 2023). A large analysis found only 43% predictivity of rodents for humans and poor-to-absent mouse–human correlation across inflammation, sepsis, burns, trauma and infection (Leist et al. 2013).

efficacy|cat.summary: Evidence is mixed: thrombolytics (tPA) in animals reduced infarct volume by 24% and improved neurobehaviour by 23% and matched clinical benefit, while corticosteroids (animal pooled OR 0.58) and tirilazad (infarct −29%, behaviour +48%) showed animal benefit but not in humans. Only <7% of studies met permissibility (Bateson's Cube) and several concordant studies involved high animal suffering.

efficacy|non-rodent.summary: Study reports toxicity concordance: non‑rodent liver concordance 40% (n=951) and animal data predicted 48% of adverse drug reactions (n=1,256); overall concordance across species was 71% (n=221). These are toxicity metrics and do not assess efficacy, so they provide too little evidence to judge non‑rodents for efficacy.

efficacy|non-human primate.summary: Evidence is mixed: some NHP results tracked clinical outcomes (thrombolysis: 24% infarct reduction and 23% neurobehavioural gain in animal models — Perel et al. 2007; HED overlap 84% — Ferreira et al. 2023), but many did not (3/494 stroke interventions; 100% AIDS‑vaccine failure — Martić‑Kehl et al. 2012).

efficacy|pig.summary: Evidence is mixed: pig efficacy studies agreed with human outcomes for bisphosphonates and thrombolytics but disagreed for corticosteroids, Tirilazad and antifibrinolytics, while antenatal corticosteroids were partially concordant; only 7% of studies were permissible by Bateson's Cube. Concordance and permissibility depended on the intervention and on animal suffering severity (moderate studies were permissible; severe were not).

efficacy|mouse.summary: Evidence is mixed: some mouse findings translated (thrombolysis reduced infarct volume 24% and bisphosphonates raised hip BMD 11% — Perel et al. 2007). But many did not—Perrin et al. 2014 found 11/12 ALS candidates failed in clinic and Pan et al. 2020 reported AUC 0.45 for TGI.

efficacy|mouse.why_range_is_wide: Translation varies by intervention, indication and study quality (e.g. published positive ALS studies vs rigorous ALS TDI null results).

efficacy|rat.summary: Evidence is mixed: rats predicted clinical efficacy for some interventions (thrombolysis reduced infarct volume 24% and improved neurobehaviour 23%; three alcohol medications originated from rat models) but failed for others (corticosteroids: animal OR 0.58 yet no human benefit; tirilazad: 29% infarct reduction in rats but clinical failure). Translation varies by drug class—bisphosphonates and thrombolytics were concordant, several CNS candidates were not.

efficacy|rabbit.summary: Evidence is mixed: some rabbit results tracked human efficacy (thrombolysis and bisphosphonates), e.g. thrombolysis in animals reduced infarct volume by 24% and improved neurobehaviour by 23%. Other interventions were discordant—corticosteroids showed animal benefit (pooled OR 0.58) but no clinical benefit; tirilazad reduced infarct 29% in animals yet failed clinically.

efficacy|sheep.summary: Sheep data are mixed: bisphosphonates raised bone density (alendronate +11.0% hip, +8.5% spine) and thrombolysis reduced infarct volume (−24%) and improved behaviour (+23%), but antenatal corticosteroids increased neonatal mortality in ewes (OR 12.5). The mortality estimate is based on seven ewe experiments and many efficacy studies involved high animal suffering, limiting permissibility.

safety-pharmacology|non-rodent.summary: Baldrick et al. 2021 report non-rodent safety‑pharmacology does not reliably predict clinical proarrhythmic risk: a stand‑alone hERG assay showed little correlation to animal data, while non‑rodent telemetry detected QTc effects in ≈10% of studies. However, the authors note in vivo telemetry can still be useful for identifying QTc effects and supporting safe clinical entry.

Little correlation — hERG assay (including low IC50 ≤1 µM) to animal cardiovascular data (Baldrick et al. 2021)

safety-pharmacology|dog.summary: Dog safety studies broadly track human cardiac and BP/HR effects: dog QTc AUC ≈0.81 (Pollard et al. 2017), 91% of human QT‑prolongers also prolonged QT in animals (Valentin et al. 2022), and combined BP/HR sensitivity/specificity were 78%/79% (Bhatt et al. 2019). However, overall discordance was 31% and nonclinical false‑negatives among TQT‑positive drugs reached 65% (Valentin et al. 2022); assay sensitivity varies by assay and exposure.

safety-pharmacology|dog.why_range_is_wide: Sensitivity varies by assay type and exposure multiple (e.g., hERG/in vivo QTc 50–57% at 30× vs APD 19%).
safety-pharmacology|dog.negative_controls_noted: Sadko et al. 2024 included a mock/vehicle negative control that produced no QTc change in dogs.

efficacy|rodent.summary: Most studies show poor translation of rodent efficacy to humans: <8% of cancer drugs entering trials translated (Mak et al. 2014) and 3 of 494 animal‑positive stroke interventions worked in patients (Martić‑Kehl et al. 2012). Some exceptions exist—Ferreira et al. 2023 found 84% HED overlap and Spanagel 2017/Sembach 2021 cite specific drug successes—but selective sampling and publication bias limit generalisability.

efficacy|rodent.why_range_is_wide: Estimates vary by disease area, outcome measured, and study selection (e.g., small/selected IB samples and publication/selective‑reporting bias).

safety-pharmacology|non-human primate.summary: Evidence is mixed: NHPs recapitulated a clinical QTc change for moxifloxacin (10.9 ms vs ~10 ms in humans; Sadko et al. 2024) and 91% of human-QT–prolonging drugs also prolonged in animals, but 31% of 150 drugs were discordant (Valentin et al. 2022). Large-animal to human BP/HR concordance was reasonable (sensitivity 78%, specificity 79%; Bhatt et al. 2019), though assay sensitivity varies by endpoint and exposure multiple.

safety-pharmacology|pig.summary: Valentin et al. 2022: nonrodent (including pig) QT findings partly tracked clinical QT—69% concordant (31% discordant, 47/150); 91% of human QT‑prolongers and 88% of human non‑prolongers matched animal results. However, sensitivity varied by assay (hERG 50%; in vivo QTc 57% at 30x; APD 19%) and 65% of TQT‑positives were nonclinical false negatives.

safety-pharmacology|rabbit.summary: Valentin et al. 2022: rabbit/nonrodent QT findings partially tracked humans — 91% of human-QT‑prolonging drugs also prolonged QT in animals and 88% of non‑prolongers had no animal effect, but 31% (47/150) of drugs were discordant. Crucially, 65% of TQT‑positive drugs were nonclinical false negatives and assay sensitivity at 30x was only 50–57%.

toxicology|mouse.summary: Mouse toxicology translates inconsistently to humans: PPV 0.57 (all grades) and 0.43 (grade 3–4) vs NPV 0.81 for grade 3–4 (Atkins et al. 2020), iNLR 1.39 (Bailey et al. 2015), though mouse cardiac LR+ = 5.29 (Clark et al. 2018). Performance varies by organ class and severity.

safety-pharmacology|rodent.summary: Rodent safety‑pharmacology tests found CNS findings in 21% and respiratory findings in 28% of studies, but none (0%) were judged of obvious concern for clinical progression; in vitro hERG assays showed little correlation with animal data even at low IC50 (≤1 µM). All figures from Baldrick et al. 2021.

toxicology|dog.summary: Dog toxicology tests are inconsistently predictive of human toxicity. Examples: Monticello et al. 2017—specificity 84% and NPV 86% (absence); Atkins et al. 2020—median dog PPV ≈0.67 and NPV ≈0.52; Bailey et al. 2019—no-animal-toxicity → 72% no human toxicity; Clark et al. 2018—dog LR+ for cardiac 6.11.

safety-pharmacology|rat.summary: Rat safety data partly track human cardiovascular outcomes: Bhatt et al. 2019 reported rat→large-animal concordance for combined BP/HR with sensitivity 84% and specificity 71% (PPV 90%, NPV 60%). However, QT findings are mixed — Valentin et al. 2022 found 91% of human QT‑prolongers also prolonged QT in animals but 31% overall discordance and only 50–57% assay sensitivity at 30x exposure.

toxicology|non-rodent.summary: Non‑rodent toxicology tracked human organ toxicities moderately: non‑rodents predicted human organ toxicity ~63% of the time (Olson et al. 2000; Wall et al. 2008) and rodent+nonrodent concordance was ~71% (Olson et al. 2000). Concordance varied by organ — e.g. non‑rodent GI 83% vs rodent GI 46% (Peters et al. 2019) — and Olson analysed only compounds with known human toxicities.

toxicology|rabbit.summary: Evidence is mixed: rabbit findings predict some human toxicities (LR+ 3.54 for cardiac, LR+ 2.8 for hepatobiliary; rabbit QT post-test odds 83%) but give little reassurance overall (rabbit median iNLR 1.12 ≈ unity). Differences reflect endpoint-specific concordance and study design/selection bias (Clark et al. 2018; Bailey et al. 2015).

LR+ 2.8 — rabbit, hepatobiliary disorders (n=101)
QT post-test odds 83% — rabbit
Median iNLR 1.12 — rabbit (near 1, little evidential weight)
toxicology|rabbit.why_range_is_wide: Endpoint-specific analyses (e.g., QT) show higher concordance while overall selectivity is low; differing datasets and selection bias explain variation.

toxicology|pig.summary: Monticello et al. 2017: animal findings predicted absence of human adverse effects better than presence — specificity 84% and NPV 86% vs sensitivity 48% and PPV 43% (clinical positive prevalence 21%). Excluding subjective 'other' events raised sensitivity to 52% and NPV to 92%.

toxicology|zebrafish.summary: Studies show zebrafish toxicology often tracks mammalian outcomes: Nikam et al. 2020 reported 100% concordance with mammalian screening and hepatotoxicity and 90% agreement for teratogenicity (n=59); Cornet et al. 2017 reported overall accuracy 78%. Performance varies by endpoint—sensitivities 54–80% and specificities 77–100% across endpoints (McGrath 2008 noted sensitivity >80% and specificity >70%).

toxicology|rodent.summary: Evidence is mixed: rodents detect some human toxicities but often miss others — rodent concordance/sensitivity ≈43–48% (Wall et al. 2008; Monticello et al. 2017; Olson et al. 2000) with mean PPV ≈36% (Bailey et al. 2019); hematologic concordance was 91% (Olson et al. 2000). Findings vary by organ, trial phase and study inclusion (e.g., Olson included only compounds with known human toxicities).

toxicology|rodent.why_range_is_wide: Estimates vary by organ system, clinical-prevalence effects on PPV/NPV, trial phase, and study inclusion criteria (e.g., Olson only included drugs with known human toxicities).

toxicology|rat.summary: Evidence is mixed: rats give modest positive signal for some toxicities (Atkins et al. 2020 median PPV 0.65; Clark et al. 2018 rat LR+ 2.74 hepatobiliary, 4.73 cardiac) but do not reliably rule out human harm (Bailey et al. 2015 rat iNLR 1.82). Jang et al. 2019 shows species mismatches (bosentan rat IC50 >100 µM vs human 10 µM).

toxicology|rat.why_range_is_wide: Metrics vary by organ class and severity of toxicity (different endpoints and study subsets produce different performance).

toxicology|non-human primate.summary: Evidence is mixed: NHPs have low-to-moderate overall predictive value for human toxicity (Monticello 2017: sens 48%, PPV 43%; Atkins 2020: median PPV 0.65, NPV 0.50; Bailey 2019: negative animal test → ~70% chance no human toxicity). Predictivity is endpoint-dependent—Clark 2018 reports LR+ up to 11 for cynomolgus monkey (cardiac/hepatobiliary).

toxicology|non-human primate.why_range_is_wide: Results differ by organ system, endpoint and study dataset/metric (some endpoints show high LR+ while many ADRs have low selectivity or iNLR≈1).

veterinary|dog.summary: Evidence is mixed: Daluwatumulle et al. 2026 found model robustness scores 31–85% across cancers (e.g. bladder 85.05%, pediatric glioma 79.88%), but Petersen‑Jones et al. 2015 reported dogs regained ERG/function close to normal while human patients showed no ERG change.
